extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, examiners, practitioners and policymakers assessing novelty and inventive step
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for what constitutes prior art and how novelty and inventive step (non‑obviousness) are assessed for patents and utility models, with discussion of means/time/place/recipient of disclosure and special exceptions across jurisdictions (Singapore, South Africa, Spain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: For information made available to the public, the disclosure must be sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to put the innovation into practice: for a product, enable the skilled person to make it; for a process, enable him to operate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notional 'person skilled in the art' is of ordinary competence but not inventive or imaginative. A disclosure that merely mentions features without enabling their practical implementation will not necessarily destroy novelty. Reverse engineering or ordinary trial-and-error steps undertaken by the skilled person can count as enabling (e.g. reverse engineering may destroy novelty), whereas extensive experiments aiming to discover undisclosed matter may indicate novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / prior publication comparison test
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine anticipation, compare the earlier publication with the patentee’s claim as at the date of publication, having regard to surrounding circumstances and without hindsight. If the prior art so construed discloses the same product/process or contains 'clear and unmistakeable directions' to the invention, the claim is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret both the prior art and the patent claim as at their respective dates (no benefit of hindsight). Use the approach from General Tire & Rubber Co v Firestone (1972) as applied in Singapore. The comparison is document-by-document.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mosaicing of prior art for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, prior art documents should be read individually when assessing novelty; 'mosaicing' (combining disclosures from multiple unconnected documents) is not permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions exist where a later document expressly refers to an earlier one or where a series of papers form a series of disclosures referring to each other. Modifications made to prior art to reach the invention are discounted for novelty; the key question is whether following the teachings of that single disclosure inevitably leads to the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inevitability test for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether an invention is anticipated by a disclosure, ask: does following the teachings in that disclosure inevitably lead to the invention? If yes, the invention is not novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If additional steps required are ordinary methods of trial and error or reverse engineering that the notional skilled person would undertake using common general knowledge, the disclosure may destroy novelty. But if the additional steps amount to experiments to discover something not disclosed, that may indicate novelty or inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing (four-step) test for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine inventive step by the Windsurfing approach: (a) identify the inventive concept embodied in the patent; (b) adopt the perspective of the normally skilled but unimaginative addressee and impute common general knowledge at the priority date; (c) identify differences between prior art and the alleged invention; (d) ask whether, without knowledge of the invention (no hindsight), those differences would have been obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structured four-step test is the primary approach cited for assessing obviousness/inventive step (Windsurfing International v Tabur Marine [1985]). Apply without ex-post-facto reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auxiliary obviousness tests: 'well‑worth trying' and 'lying on the road'
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional indicia for obviousness include (i) the 'well‑worth trying' test — an invention is obvious if the skilled person would have felt it was well worth trying to solve a problem or achieve a beneficial result; and (ii) the 'lying on the road' test — the invention is obvious if prior art was 'lying on the road' and available for the research worker to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are supplementary, practical tests courts have applied to assess whether the skilled person would have had sufficient motive/confidence to make the claimed changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'state of the art' / prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'state of the art' comprises all matter which has at any time before the priority date been made available to the public, in oral or written form or by use or any other way (jurisdiction-specific statutory formulations cited: e.g. Singapore Sec.14/15 summary; South Africa Patents Act Sec.25; Spain SPL Art.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This broad definition means manner, time, extent or place of disclosure are generally irrelevant so long as it was made before the priority date and was 'available to the public', subject to statutory exceptions (confidentiality, certain grace/excused disclosures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pending (unpublished) patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending patent applications which have not yet been published may affect novelty (they can be part of the prior art) but generally do not affect inventive step; jurisdictions vary on precise treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions (e.g., South Africa Sec.25(7); Spain Art.6.3 SPL / EPC Art.54.3) determine when unpublished or pending applications are treated as prior art — typically included for novelty if they have an earlier priority date and are open to public inspection, but excluded when assessing inventive step in many systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret commercial use treated differently for novelty vs inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret use of an invention on a commercial scale within the territory may be deemed part of the state of the art for purposes of novelty, but treatment for inventive step may differ depending on statutory wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: South African law (Sec.25(8)) treats secret commercial use as part of the state of the art for novelty. However, some statutory schemes exclude secret uses from the narrower prior art considered for inventive step — check local statute/case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means, time and place of disclosure usually irrelevant
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement that availability be by a particular means, method, mode, or to a large section of the public; the manner, time or place of disclosure is usually irrelevant provided it occurred before the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidental disclosure, oral disclosure, or limited-audience disclosures can still count as prior art if they were 'available to the public'. The exact legal construction of 'availability' may be influenced by conflict-of-law principles when the patent is for a particular country (e.g., Singapore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and disclosures to specific recipients
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures made in breach of confidence or unlawfully obtained from the inventor/proprietor, or disclosures made under conditions of confidentiality (express or implied), are to be disregarded and do not form part of the public prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: disclosures due to unlawful acquisition or breach of confidence; displays at international exhibitions may be disregarded if appropriate declarations and evidence are filed (time-limited grace/excusal rules apply, e.g., within 12 months in some contexts). Encryption/passwords or payment obligations are strong evidence of intended confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excusable disclosures by applicant / reasonable trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain disclosures do not invalidate a patent if they were made without the patentee's knowledge/consent or were reasonable technical trials/experiments by the applicant (statutory excusals such as South Africa Sec.26(a)/(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: South African Sec.26(b) excuses disclosure by way of reasonable technical trial or experiment in the Republic when made by the applicant or predecessor. Sec.26(a) excuses disclosures acquired from the applicant without his/her knowledge if the applicant subsequently applied for protection with reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic / internet disclosure treated as prior art if publicly accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Paperless information (internet postings, electronic records) can constitute sufficient disclosure to affect novelty and inventive step, provided it was made available to the public before the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility, evidence and persistence are practical issues: encrypted or paywalled material may still be public; transient electronic availability is harder to prove as prior art. Courts consider nature of network, access/security settings and reasonable expectation of confidentiality. Rules of admissibility for computer records (e.g. Evidence Act provisions) may affect reliance on such prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure and scope of 'public' depending on technical complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a disclosure is 'available to the public' may depend on the nature of the invention: for highly technical inventions the 'public' may be interpreted to include only addressees in the technical field; disclosure must be an 'enabling disclosure' to count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: South African common law and EPO policy referenced: state of the art includes anything it was possible for the public to gain knowledge of and which may be freely disclosed without breach of confidence. Information obtainable by disassembly or reverse engineering typically constitutes disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different treatment of patents vs utility models
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal standards and territorial scope of prior art differ between patents and utility models: patents generally require absolute novelty worldwide; utility models may be subject to territorial novelty rules and a lower inventive activity threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spain: patents — prior art = everything accessible worldwide; utility models — prior art limited to disclosures within Spain. Inventive activity for patents requires non-evidentness to the expert; utility models require that the solution is not 'very evident' (less stringent). Procedural differences also exist for certificates of addition and for inclusion/exclusion of unpublished applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and practical evidentiary problems with internet and digital prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical problems of proof arise with internet and digital disclosures; the burden of proof generally rests with the party asserting the prior art and difficulties include proving timing, persistence and exact content of electronic disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing admissibility of computer records and reliable provenance is necessary. Courts may require compliance with statutory evidence rules; transient online content may be difficult to rely on as prior art even if legally qualifying as disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory provisions and case law guide jurisdictional nuances
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute and case law together determine precise rules in each jurisdiction (examples cited: Singapore Patents Act provisions and cases; South Africa Patents Act Secs.25/26 and case law; Spain SPL articles aligned with EPC), including specific inclusions/exclusions for prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must consult local statute and leading cases for application (e.g., scope of subsections, treatment of pending applications, grace/excusal rules, and interpretation of 'available to the public'). National differences (e.g., territorial limits for utility models, statutory excusals for technical trials) are significant.
